text.p: Colin Montgomerie finished the European season raging at officials for "bringing the game into disrepute" and slamming what he called "the worst golf hole we played all year".
Alhough Montgomerie proved himself the best player on the Tour for the fourth time, his efforts were overshadowed at the end by a farcical incident involving the player placed third.

Australian Robert Allenby fractured his sternum in a car crash four weeks ago yet made a 40,000 km round trip from Melbourne to hit one shot at the Volvo Masters for the chance of a $116,500 bonus. The rules said he had to play to qualify for the place money.
Allenby, a winner three times before his accident, dribbled his shot 35 yards and withdrew from the tournament, saying the money would go to charity.
It made Montgomerie's title-clinching first shot later that Thursday almost insignificant.
That Allenby's effort turned out to be enough to keep him in third position when the scores of his rivals were totted up on Sunday was virtually irrelevant.
Montgomerie spoke for many when he said of the ruling: "It is bringing the game into disrepute. It is a farce. We are holding ourselves up to ridicule.
Montgomerie was equally scathing on Sunday about the 17th hole at Valderrama, a course that has staged its last Masters although it hosts next year's Ryder Cup.
Although he made a par five with a good chip and a putt, he was irritated that his second shot with a seven-iron from the rough struck the green and trickled back down into the lake in front.
"Can you believe that? It is not on. I have had a good record here but since they changed the 17th hole the golf course is gone for me," he said.
"A shot like that could decide the Ryder Cup. That should not happen."
None of which detracted from his golf through the year, which left the Scot able to finish an uninspiring joint 29th at Valderrama after four years in the top four including victory in 1993.
His start to the season was brilliant by comparison after being delayed until March when his wife Eimear gave birth to their second child. Montgomerie used the time to shed 15 kg.

He won his first event, the Dubai Desert Classic, by one stroke, almost won the Players' Championship on the U.S. Tour two weeks later and secured his second victory in June in the Irish Open at Druid's Glen.

Then came a major slump beginning with an 81 in the windswept final round of the Scottish Open at Carnoustie and continuing at the British Open at Royal Lytham, where he missed the cut for the fourth time in five years.
"I tend to leave my worst rounds of the golf year to the third week in July," he said.
He missed another cut three weeks later at the U.S. PGA championship.
"My slump lasted a few weeks. Most people's last longer. I missed cuts in two majors, then I started winning again," he said.
He set all kinds of records with closing scores of 61-63 to win the European Masters in Switzerland in September for his third title of the year.
When lone challenger Ian Woosnam missed the cut at the German Masters last month, Montgomerie was home and dry as Europe's number one again, but lacking inspiration.
He lost all his matches as Scotland crashed out of the Dunhill Cup and lost in the World Matchplay second round.
Woosnam, won four tournaments before back trouble thwarted his chance of the top spot and left him facing surgery during the off-season.

Bernhard Langer lost two notable records. His string of surviving 68 halfway cuts in Europe ended at the Volvo PGA. He was left empty-handed after winning at least once every year for 16 successive years.
Ryder Cup captain Seve Ballesteros endured a miserable year finishing 69th on the money list, his worst since his first year as a professional in 1974.
Youngsters emerged and Thomas Bjorn of Denmark is favourite for the Rookie of the Year award after his victory in the Loch Lomond Invitational last month.
